posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value CRO post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the auditability problem from a product angle, position explainability as the real unlock without pitching
posts.draft_comment: The ban makes complete sense to me. It's not really an AI problem — it's a lineage problem. If you can't trace a number back to its source data, step by step, it doesn't matter how good the answer looks. Regulators don't accept confidence intervals, they want a paper trail.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with Power BI adoption failure — validate the pain hard, then reframe the real problem as trust not tools
posts.draft_comment: 18 months is brutal, but honestly the Excel exports aren't the problem — they're just the symptom. Finance teams revert because they don't know *whose* logic is inside the numbers, and they can't defend something they can't trace. A dashboard that looks right and a dashboard someone will stake their reputation on in front of a board are completely different things. How did you handle it when they asked where a number came from?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why nobody uses it' layer without pitching
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically a confession that nobody agreed on what actually matters. The usage jump to 85% isn't really about fewer metrics — it's that five things people trust beats fifty things nobody owns. We keep blaming the tools but the real problem is dashboards built to impress the person who commissioned them, not the person who has to act on Monday morning. What made those five the ones that survived the cut?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging on self-service BI failure — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the governance-before-tooling insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports problem isn't a Power BI problem — it's what happens when you hand out tools before anyone's agreed on the definitions underneath them. Tooling just scales whatever's already broken. I'd actually flip the question slightly: it's not who owns the truth, it's who's allowed to *change* it — because that's where the real fights happen. Have you found anyone in your org who actually wants that job?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org reframing AI hallucinations as security risk, not just accuracy — validate the reframe, add the governance layer insight, ICP prospect (CEO at SecureData) is watching
posts.draft_comment: The framing shift here is the important bit — hallucinated outputs aren't just wrong, they're unverified inputs into decisions, which is exactly how we'd describe a security vulnerability. Most analytics teams are still treating this as a QA problem when it's really a trust chain problem. Who owns that chain when the output leaves the tool and enters a boardroom?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post nailing the exact pain Milo solves — validate the diagnosis hard, add the deeper reason why it keeps happening, no pitch needed
posts.draft_comment: That £200k story is so common it's almost a cliché now — and yet it keeps happening. The dirty secret is most platforms are optimised for the person building the dashboards, not the person who's supposed to make a decision at 8am on a Monday. Vendors demo to data teams, data teams love it, then six months later the CFO is still asking someone to pull numbers manually. Who actually owns the gap between 'we have a BI tool' and 'our team uses it'?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial firm naming a real data governance failure — validate the cultural diagnosis and add the layer most people skip over
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, one dataset, three different truths. That's not a data problem, that's a decision problem — nobody agreed who owns the definition before the dashboard went live. Culture fix is right, but the culture conversation usually needs a concrete moment to happen around. Did the CFO leave that meeting wanting to fix the process, or just fix the number?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' adoption failure — validate the underlying problem that the tool assumes users know what they need, which is the real gap
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is brutal but honest. Most BI and AI tools assume people already know what question to ask — they just need help answering it faster. But that's not where the friction is. The friction is one step earlier: figuring out what's even worth asking in the first place.
